points: Consumer Price Index inflation in India frequently tests the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance threshold of 6%, driven mainly by volatile food components.
The author argues that interventions usually arrive late after food shocks have depleted household savings and triggered broader price pressures.
Food inflation is regressive, forcing lower-income deciles who spend 45% to 60% of their expenditure on food to suffer a severe loss in real purchasing power.
Vulnerable households cope by substituting protein-rich foods with cheaper, starch-heavy alternatives, worsening child malnutrition and anaemia while unorganised workers lack indexed wage protection.
Smallholders face a disconnect where retail surges do not translate to higher real incomes due to intermediaries, mandi cartels, and rising input costs of diesel, electricity, and seeds.
High living costs suppress Private Final Consumption Expenditure and force fiscal trade-offs by increasing welfare demands, which diverts public funds from capital expenditure.
Persistent headline inflation keeps the RBI's repo rate elevated under the Flexible Inflation Targeting framework, raising borrowing costs for MSMEs and slowing industrial investment.

Proposals to contain inflation include expanding PDS safety nets, using digital market surveillance, enforcing stock limits under the Essential Commodities Act, and strengthening farm-to-fork chains via the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund.
sum.text:
General Studies-3; Topic: Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilization of resources, growth, development and employment.
Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation in India frequently tests the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) upper tolerance threshold of 6%, primarily triggered by volatile food components.
While statistical base effects periodically pull headline numbers down, retail prices of essentials (vegetables, pulses, edible oils) remain high, straining household budgets.
Interventions typically arrive late—after food shocks have depleted household savings and fed into broader price pressures. Proactive administrative and market mitigation must precede monetary tightening.
Regressive Nature of Food Inflation: Lower-income deciles allocate between 45% and 60% of their expenditure to food. A surge in basic food prices sharply reduces real purchasing power. Nutritional Strains: Vulnerable households often cope by substituting protein-rich foods (pulses, dairy, eggs) with cheaper, starch-heavy alternatives, worsening child malnutrition and anaemia. The Informal Sector Gap: Unlike formal sector workers whose wages adjust through dearness allowances, unorganised workers lack indexed wage protection.

sum.text:
India ranks third globally in the number of large dams (over 5,700 registered structures), behind only China and the United States.
Post-independence policy viewed large multipurpose river valley projects—such as Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, and Nagarjuna Sagar—as essential engines of growth. Jawaharlal Nehru famously called them the “temples of modern India.”
Changing climate patterns, extreme precipitation events, structural ageing, and heavy siltation have transformed many reservoirs from flood buffers into flood accelerants and drivers of riverine degradation.
Agricultural Resilience: Large dams underpin the Green Revolution. By storing surplus southwest monsoon run-off, they provide perennial surface irrigation across drought-prone basins like the Indus, Krishna, and Godavari.

Nearly two months after Nepal suffered devastating floods, the UN climate convention’s Fund for Loss and Damage (FLD) has allocated $21.6 million to the Himalayan nation. This is the first time that the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. Kathmandu had invoked the principle of climate justice in its application: Nepal accounts for barely 0.1 per cent of global emissions, yet it is on the frontline of climate change in the Himalaya. The ice-and-rock avalanche that triggered flash floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems claimed more than 1,400 lives, several villages were swept away, and the country lost at least 10 per cent of its hydropower facilities. Conservative estimates put Nepal’s recovery and reconstruction requirements at $5 billion. The grant, far short of what Nepal needs, marks an important first step in turning the commitment of climate reparation into action.
Established at the UNFCCC’s COP27 in 2022 and operationalised a year later, the FLD is a product of a nearly three-decade-long campaign by nations most vulnerable to global warming. It rests on the principle of climate compensation, not charity. This distinction is not academic. The Global North is often willing to provide humanitarian assistance, but a fund explicitly meant to address “loss and damage” remains fraught because it raises questions related to responsibility for climate change. Nepal’s application ran into predictable bureaucratic hurdles. The FLD’s application window had closed in June, and when Nepal sought emergency funding, claims from 119 countries were awaiting approval. Developed countries initially argued that granting Kathmandu’s request would mean allowing it to jump the queue. sum.text: Is AI crowding out other investments? Paul Krugman recently wrote that it is 'crowding out other potential uses of capital'. At first glance, data appear to support his argument. US hyperscalers like Amazon, Google and Microsoft are pouring unprecedented sums into AI with capex expected to reach $800 bn in 2026. Yet, overall investment has barely budged. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study estimates that gross domestic investment in the US accounted for 21.3% of GDP in the 5 yrs before Covid. Since 2022, when companies began investing heavily in AI, the share has edged up to just 21.5%. Also read: Is the AI boom real or a bubble? Nikhil Kamath asks Silicon Valley founders So, to conclude from these data that AI is crowding out other investments is misleading. The argument assumes the economy has a limited pool of capital and every dollar invested in AI is a dollar unavailable to other sectors. For an open economy like the US, this assumption is highly questionable. Capital can flow in from abroad, and higher expected returns can attract additional financing rather than simply redirect existing funds. The argument also rests on a distinction between AI and non-AI investments that becomes increasingly difficult to sustain if AI is, indeed, the transformative technology its proponents claim it to be. AI is not just another sector competing with healthcare, education, manufacturing and agriculture for investment dollars. Its promise lies precisely in its ability to transform these sectors. If AI raises productivity across the economy, spending on AI cannot be neatly separated from investment in the industries that benefit from it. The distinction may make sense in accounting statements. But it becomes less useful when assessing the broader economic consequences of that spending. Consider healthcare. If AI makes surgery more precise, reduces medical errors and enables better diagnoses, investment in AI would also be an investment in healthcare's productive capacity. Elon Musk has gone further, predicting that AI and humanoid robots will revolutionise medicine, making the best healthcare virtually free and superior to what even world leaders receive today. Musk may be exaggerating. Whether or not his vision materialises, the underlying point stands: value of AI investment may ultimately be realised in sectors far removed from the companies developing the technology. I n early October, several stakeholders, including families with children studying abroad, importers awaiting shipments, and motorists monitoring fuel prices, experienced heightened anxiety. On Friday, 9 October, the Indian rupee closed the week at about Rs 96.7 to the dollar, near the record low seen in May. At the same time, India’s foreign exchange reserves had declined for five consecutive weeks, foreign investors had consistently divested from Indian equities, and oil prices had exceeded $100 per barrel. Subsequently, the Reserve Bank of India quietly implemented strategic changes, and, within a week, the rupee appreciated to nearly Rs 95. The RBI’s intervention targeted rapid capital movement. It reduced the permissible size of currency derivative transactions lacking an underlying trade from $100 million to $5 million, prohibited companies from cancelling and rebooking hedges for speculative purposes, mandated banks to maintain a 20 per cent cash reserve with the RBI against large forward dollar purchase contracts, and established a special facility to sell dollars directly to state-run oil companies, thereby excluding their transactions from the open market. Although these measures were not explicitly termed capital controls, they effectively function as such, and their effectiveness will influence the rupee’s trajectory in the coming months. Six weeks that emptied the cushion To understand the rationale behind the RBI’s actions, it helps to examine developments during the summer. Between mid-July and early September, foreign exchange reserves increased by approximately $110 billion over seven weeks, reaching a record high of $785.7 billion on 4 September. This significant increase reflected a major capital influx, including special dollar deposits from Indians abroad, which, as I noted in my September column , attracted far more funds than anticipated. Over time, service teams find themselves looking after equipment of different ages, often across several states and under very different operating conditions. We have seen this at WattPower as our installed base has grown to 24+ GW across 16 states. Supporting a handful of projects in one region is relatively straightforward.
Things become more complicated when installations are spread across the country. Distance is only part of the challenge. A plant operating in Rajasthan's extreme heat will have different support needs from one exposed to coastal humidity.
Equipment age and site conditions also influence how often service teams need to step in. The service network must be able to keep up with the equipment already operating in the field.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (PTI) The Supreme Court on Tuesday sought the Centre's response on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) challenging the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025.
The association, which represents 21 prominent news organisations, has said that the law, which carries no exemption for journalism, could cripple news gathering and dilute the citizen's right to information.
The law, passed by Parliament in August 2023, is the first comprehensive legislation on the protection of digital personal data. It requires any entity processing personal data, termed a "Data Fiduciary", to do so either with the consent of the individual concerned or for a limited set of "legitimate uses" listed in Section 7 of the DPDP Act, which provides for the legitimate uses of data.
It says a Data Fiduciary may process personal data of a Data Principal for any of the following uses, namely: "(a) for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal has voluntarily provided her personal data to the Data Fiduciary, and in respect of which she has not indicated to the Data Fiduciary that she does not consent to the use of her personal data."
Breaches can attract penalties of up to Rs 250 crore.
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified the accompanying Rules on November 13, 2025, with implementation to be staggered over 18 months.
At the heart of the challenge is the absence of any carve-out for news reporting, which finds no place either among the legitimate uses in Section 7 or the exemptions in Section 17.
Section 17 lists out instances where personal data protection does not apply and they include legal claims where personal data is processed to enforce a legal right or claim.

texts.x: The UNFCCC’s 2026 NDC Synthesis Report found that even full implementation, including conditional pledges, would cut emissions only 9% below 2019 levels by 2035

points: A UN report released on Tuesday stated that current climate pledges will cut global greenhouse gas emissions by only 6 percent below 2019 levels by 2035.
Even with conditional elements fully implemented, emissions are projected to drop by just 9 percent below 2019 levels by 2035.
This projected reduction is substantially off track compared to the dip required to limit global warming effectively.
The 2026 Nationally Determined Contributions Synthesis Report was published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.
Findings are based on 127 new NDCs representing 154 parties to the 2015 Paris Agreement, submitted between January 1, 2024, and August 31, 2026.
Most new NDCs target net-zero emissions between 2040 and 2070, with the majority aiming for 2050.
Implementation of these targets implies a best-estimate warming of 1.7 to 2.3 degrees Celsius by the end of the century.
Returning warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius requires substantial additional greenhouse gas emission reductions in coming years.
sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (PTI) If countries implement their current climate pledges, global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are expected to drop only 6 per cent below 2019 levels by 2035, meaning the projected reduction is substantially off track, compared to the dip required to limit global warming, a UN report released on Tuesday said. The ‘2026 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) Synthesis Report’ by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) said even if these commitments — called NDCs — are fully implemented, including conditional elements, emissions are likely to be just 9 per cent below 2019 levels by 2035. The report comes days after another UN report revealed that the 1.5-degree Celsius temperature target was now completely out of reach. It also stated that the best the world could do is restrict the global rise in temperatures to 1.8 degrees Celsius and try to pull it back. Show Full Article

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojna (BHAVYA) with an outlay of ₹33,660 crore to develop 100 plug-and-play industrial parks across the country.
The scheme is aimed at boosting manufacturing, attracting investments and generating large-scale employment, forming a key pillar of India’s vision for a ‘Viksit Bharat’ and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
BHAVYA will focus on developing modern, ready-to-use industrial ecosystems, building on the success of industrial smart cities under the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme (NICDP).
The initiative will be implemented in partnership with states and private players, with parks ranging in size from 100 to 1,000 acres.
Financial assistance of up to ₹1 crore per acre will be provided for core infrastructure such as roads, utilities, drainage and ICT systems; value-added facilities including factory sheds, testing labs and warehousing; and social infrastructure like worker housing and support amenities.
Additional support of up to 25% of project cost will be extended for external connectivity infrastructure.
A key feature of the scheme is its emphasis on streamlined approvals and single-window clearances, enabling industries to move quickly from planning to production.
With pre-approved land, ready infrastructure and integrated services, BHAVYA aims to significantly reduce entry barriers for investors and improve the ease of doing business.
Project selection will be carried out through a challenge-based mechanism, ensuring that only high-quality, investment-ready proposals are approved.
The industrial parks will be aligned with PM GatiShakti principles, ensuring seamless multimodal connectivity and efficient logistics.
They will also incorporate green energy solutions; sustainable resource management; and underground utility corridors to enable a no-dig environment.
The government said the scheme will generate significant direct and indirect employment across manufacturing, logistics and services sectors, while catalysing investments nationwide.
By promoting cluster-based development, BHAVYA will encourage co-location of industries, suppliers and service providers, strengthening domestic supply chains and supporting regional industrialisation.
The scheme will benefit MSMEs, startups, large manufacturers and global investors, while also creating opportunities for workers, logistics providers and local communities.

explain.headline: Parliament passes Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill, 2026
static: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act (MMDR Act) regulates the mining sector in India and specifies the requirement and procedure for obtaining mining leases.

Entry 54 of the Union List (List I) in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution empowers Parliament to legislate on regulation of mines and mineral development to the extent specified in public interest.
Entry 23 of the State List (List II) subjects the regulation of mines and mineral development to the provisions of the Union List enacted by Parliament.
Major minerals include coal, lignite, atomic minerals, and metallic ores like iron ore, copper, and manganese, while minor minerals include building stones, gravel, and ordinary clay.
The Central Government frames rules for major mineral concessions under the MMDR framework, while state governments frame rules for minor minerals.

The Lok Sabha cleared the legislation on Wednesday and the Rajya Sabha passed it on Thursday, awaiting presidential assent to become law.
Union Mines Minister G Kishan Reddy stated the Bill aims to ensure uniform mineral rates nationwide without interfering with states' revenue autonomy.
The Centre will regulate major minerals like coal, limestone, iron ore, copper, and manganese, while states retain powers over 49 minor minerals.
Coal remains crucial for India, accounting for 73 percent of electricity generation and requiring reliable supply to keep industry competitive.

sum.text:
Parliament on Thursday passed the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, which seeks to restrict the power of state governments to levy taxes on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands.
The Lok Sabha had passed the Bill on Wednesday, while the Rajya Sabha cleared it on Thursday, completing the parliamentary approval process. The legislation will come into force after receiving the President’s assent.
Replying to the debate in the Rajya Sabha, Union Mines Minister G Kishan Reddy said the legislation does not seek to interfere with the autonomy or revenue rights of states, but aims to ensure uniformity in mineral rates across the country.
Reddy said the Centre would regulate major minerals such as coal, limestone, iron ore, copper and manganese, while states would continue to exercise powers over 49 minor minerals.
Defending the legislation, the Minister said coal remains crucial for India’s power sector, accounting for 73 per cent of electricity generation. He said reliable electricity supply was essential for maintaining the competitiveness of Indian industry.
Reddy also said the share of mineral revenue accruing to states had increased from 65 per cent in 2014-15 to 85 per cent currently, while the states’ share of coal revenue had risen from 51 per cent to 96 per cent.
He said the Centre receives about 11 per cent of mineral revenue, with around 88 per cent going to states, and asserted that no state would suffer revenue losses as a result of the amendment.
The Minister referred to Entry 54 of the Union List, which empowers Parliament to regulate mines and mineral development in the public interest, and said taxation was an important instrument for regulating and developing the sector.
The debate on the Bill took place amid sloganeering by Opposition MPs, who have been demanding the presence of Union Home Minister Amit Shah in Parliament over concerns regarding alleged police action against students protesting at Jantar Mantar over the medical entrance examination paper leak.
Opposition members also raised slogans over allegations concerning the theft of donations made to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.
The Bill was passed after the Rajya Sabha rejected by voice vote an amendment moved by DMK MP Tiruchi Siva seeking to refer the legislation to a Select Committee of the House.

explain.headline: Thailand Advances Carbon Capture Framework to Meet Net-Zero Goals
static: Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) involves capturing carbon dioxide emissions from fuel combustion or industrial processes, preventing their release into the atmosphere.
Captured carbon can be recycled for industrial use such as in enhanced oil recovery, synthetic fuels, and building materials, or permanently stored in deep underground geological formations.
CCUS is considered vital for decarbonising hard-to-abate sectors like steel, cement, chemicals, and power generation where direct electrification is difficult.
Major technological components include capture technologies (post-combustion, pre-combustion, and oxy-fuel), transport pipelines, and safe geological storage sites.

explain.why_in_news: The first meeting of Thailand's panel to drive greenhouse gas reduction through applied CCUS technology was recently held under the Energy Minister.
explain.background: CCUS technologies capture industrial CO2 emissions either to permanently store them underground or repurpose them into commercial products, serving as a critical tool for hard-to-abate sectors.
significance: Highlights how developing nations are creating dedicated legal and tax frameworks to scale up unproven industrial carbon management technologies.
Demonstrates the integration of carbon capture as a pillar in national power development plans and net-zero emission timelines.
Serves as a relevant case study for emerging economies like India aiming to balance industrial growth with deep decarbonisation in hard-to-abate sectors.

explain.headline: India Reaffirms Commitment to Biodiversity Conservation at CBD COP-17 in Yerevan
static: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is a legally binding multilateral treaty for the conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources.
The CBD was opened for signature at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and entered into force in 1993.
The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the governing body of the Convention, advancing its implementation through regular decisions.
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) was adopted at CBD COP15, setting ambitious global targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

India enacted the Biological Diversity Act in 2002 to give effect to the provisions of the CBD, establishing a three-tier institutional framework comprising the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees.
explain.what: Union Minister Shri Bhupender Yadav delivered India's National Statement at CBD COP-17 in Yerevan, Armenia, highlighting India's targets, conservation networks, and demands for predictable climate finance.

sum.text:
Tightening liquidity in the banking system has pushed up short-term borrowing rates and prompted the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to inject funds into banks, while rising oil prices are adding pressure on government bond yields, according to a report by ICICI Bank. The report said the banking system’s surplus liquidity fell sharply due to Goods and Services Tax (GST) payments, higher cash reserve requirements and other factors. The surplus stood at Rs 50,000 crore, or 0.2 per cent of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), as of October 23.
“System liquidity surplus declined sharply on account of outflows for GST payments, which led to the RBI conducting VRR operations,” the report said. The RBI has started conducting variable-rate repo (VRR) auctions to provide short-term funds to banks, including a seven-day operation worth Rs 1 lakh crore, the report added.
The tighter cash position pushed the weekly average call rate, the rate at which banks borrow from one another for short periods, to 5.70 per cent from 5.48 per cent in the previous week. The average market repo rate also rose to 5.66 per cent from 5.37 per cent, while the triparty repo rate increased to 5.65 per cent from 5.55 per cent. ICICI Bank expects the RBI to continue these liquidity operations. However, government spending towards the end of the month and the maturity of government securities worth Rs 35,400 crore could release funds into the banking system, easing pressure on short-term rates.
Government bond yields have also come under pressure as oil prices rise amid the ongoing conflict in West Asia, raising concerns about inflation and the possibility of higher interest rates. Weak demand at the Centre’s government securities auction reflected negative market sentiment, the report said. The average cost of government borrowing at the auction rose by 20 basis points to 7.60 per cent, while the bid-to-cover ratio stood at 1.9, below the long-term average of 2.8. The ratio measures demand for government securities against the amount offered.
ICICI Bank expects the 10-year benchmark government bond yield to trade between 7.40 per cent and 7.60 per cent in the near term. It cautioned that elevated oil prices could weigh on bond prices. Markets will also watch the US Federal Reserve’s policy decision this week, along with decisions by the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan and US third-quarter GDP data, the report said.

Twenty one news publishers, including large media companies like The Hindu, Times of India, Indian Express, Mathrubhumi, Manorama, India Today, NDTV and Network18 have approached the court through DNPA. The DNPA, which represents the publishers, has sought the removal of provisions it says threaten press freedom.
Several media organisations like Reporters Collective and Digipub had already challenged the law. The petition, filed by DNPA on October 6, challenges parts of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the rules notified in 2025. It is among the most prominent legal challenges to the law, which is intended to regulate the processing of individuals’ digital personal data. Most of the disputed provisions are scheduled to take effect in May 2027.
Their challenge centres on the absence of a specific exemption for journalistic work, despite assurances from the government that press freedom would be protected. The DNPA argues that the law could force reporters to seek permission from people they are investigating before processing their personal information. Such a requirement, it says, could alert those under scrutiny and give them an opportunity to destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses before a story is published.
The association has also questioned provisions allowing individuals to withdraw consent and demand the erasure of their personal data. The petition challenges Section 36 of the Act, read with Rule 23 and the Seventh Schedule of the rules, which empower the Union government to seek information from organisations handling personal data. N Chandrasekaran, Chairman of Tata Sons, emphasized the dual challenge India faces in decarbonizing while simultaneously industrializing and expanding prosperity. He noted that conventional finance alone won't suffice, underscoring the need for capital willing to take early risks and accept lower near-term returns for long-term gains.
He believes that with the right financial structure, India's climate transition can drive innovation and energy security. The report also points out that the amount of catalytic capital needed varies by technology maturity. For instance, mature solar energy requires less catalytic capital due to its established track record, while nascent green hydrogen needs more support for equity and risk-sharing.
To further boost financing, the report recommends establishing a National Green Finance Institution, as suggested by NITI Aayog, to pool catalytic capital from various sources. The Election Commission of India's counter affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on Monday, relied heavily on Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The commission states that its three orders on the special intensive revision (SIR), issued on June 24, 2025, October 27, 2025 and May 14, 2026, were made unanimously. The Opposition petitioners, led by Rahul Gandhi, argue that the commission’s collective powers were exercised unilaterally by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. What the section saysSection 18 has two parts. Sub-section1 allows the commission, by unanimous decision, to regulate the procedure for transacting its business and to allocate that business among the CEC and the other commissioners. Sub-section (2) deals with the decisions themselves. All business must be transacted unanimously “as far as possible”, and if the CEC and the other commissioners differ, the matter is decided according to the majority opinion. In a three-member commission, this means that two commissioners can prevail over the third, including the CEC. Under Article 324(3), the CEC is the commission's chairman, but the 2023 law gives the chair neither a veto nor a casting vote. Not a new ruleSection 10 of the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991, had identical language. The 2023 Act changed the appointment process for the CEC and election commissioners and added Section 16. That section protects a person who is or was CEC or an election commissioner from civil or criminal proceedings for acts done or words spoken while discharging their functions. Petitioners have argued in court that this immunity did not exist in the earlier law, making the question of collective decision making more important. What the ECI says.

sum.text:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra advised State governments to adopt prudent borrowing strategies, maintain quality expenditure and manage cash efficiently at the 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries in Mumbai on 27 October 2026. The conference theme was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’.
Fiscal sustainability refers to a government’s ability to meet its spending and debt obligations over time. State borrowing finances expenditure but adds to public debt and future repayment obligations. Quality of expenditure concerns the effectiveness and intended outcomes of public spending. Cash management involves planning government receipts and payments to meet obligations on time and manage temporary cash mismatches.
Malhotra urged States to combine prudent borrowing with efficient cash management. He also released the Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments, which covers concepts, operational processes and practices related to State cash and debt management.
The State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) is a State-level forum for coordination between banks, government departments and other stakeholders. Malhotra urged States to make effective use of the SLBC forum. He also encouraged States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI), a digital platform intended to facilitate access to credit through the sharing of relevant financial information.
Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is digital money issued by a central bank. Programmable CBDC can have conditions attached to its use. Malhotra encouraged States to use Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT), through which government benefits are transferred directly to beneficiaries.
The conference reviewed market borrowings by States, short-term financial accommodation from the RBI and adoption of a Benchmark Issuance Strategy. Such a strategy involves issuing debt securities at specified benchmark maturities to support a more regular borrowing pattern.
Finance secretaries from 27 States and three Union Territories attended the conference, along with senior officials from the Union Ministry of Finance, the Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.

This amendment was triggered by judicial setbacks in the Bombay and Punjab and Haryana High Courts which questioned the legal basis for requisitioning private staff.
The core legal debate centers on whether subordinate rules can exceed the parent Census Act, 1948, and if the government can legally compel private individuals to serve.

sum.text:
Private Citizens for Census Duty Latest News Recently, the Centre amended the Census Rules, 1990, to explicitly include teachers of private educational institutions and employees of private establishments (banks, companies, societies, trusts) as eligible Census enumerators. This has reignited a legal debate: can the government legally compel private individuals to perform Census duties — and why was this amendment needed if the old rules already allowed “any person” to be appointed? What the Amendment Actually Changes The amended rules now expressly name teachers of government, local authority, aided, and unaided private institutions as eligible enumerators.
It also retains the broader category: any person whom a state/UT government considers suitable. Crucially, this isn’t very different from before — the earlier Rule 3 already allowed enumerators to be chosen from “Teachers, Clerks or any official or any person.” MHA’s stated reason: to remove ambiguity and ensure smooth conduct of the Census, which needs lakhs of enumerators. The Legal Backdrop That Triggered This May 2026: The Bombay High Court gave interim protection to over 500 private unaided and minority schools in Maharashtra, holding that Sections 6 and 7 of the Census Act did not confer authority to compulsorily requisition staff of private unaided schools, unlike Section 4A, which binds local authorities.
The court rejected the government’s argument that “any person” under the old rules covered private teachers, warning this interpretation could extend unrestricted even to doctors, advocates, and chartered accountants. It held, prima facie, that subordinate legislation (rules) cannot exceed its parent statute (the Act). October 2026: The Punjab and Haryana High Court stayed Haryana government communications seeking private-school teacher details for Census duty.
Later, the Centre issued the amendment — seen as a response to these judicial setbacks. sum.text:
India, Oct. 27 -- A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed and exchanged on 26 October 2026 in Paris between the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and the Bibliotheque nationale de France (BnF) (National Library of France), under Gyan Bharatam Mission, to strengthen institutional cooperation in the preservation, digitisation, research and dissemination of manuscript and documentary heritage. The MoU was signed by Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and Mr Gilles Pecout, President of BnF.
Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and Gilles Pecout, President of Bibliotheque nationale de France
The partnership brings together the Ministry of Culture, through Gyan Bharatam, National Archives of India, New Delhi, and National Library, Kolkata, and BnF. It establishes a framework for cooperation across five key areas: Digitisation; Cross-Sharing on the National Digital Repository; Technology Exchange; Conservation; and Research & Development.
The Ministry of Culture and BnF will work to identify and digitise Indic-origin manuscripts and collections held by BnF. The MoU further provides for exchange of expertise and knowledge in areas such as digitisation and preservation technologies, cataloguing standards, OCR/HTR tools for Indian scripts, digital humanities and manuscript conservation. Joint workshops, capacity-building programmes, research initiatives, publications, exhibitions and exchanges of scholars and experts have also been envisaged under the partnership.
Gyan Bharatam Mission is the Ministry of Culture's flagship initiative dedicated to the identification, documentation, conservation, digitisation, translation, research and dissemination of India's manuscript heritage. Its National Digital Repository is envisaged as a secure digital repository for Indian-origin manuscripts and Indian Knowledge Systems held in India and across the world, enabling structured, permission-based access for research and study.
Bridging centuries of knowledge and heritage, the partnership marks an important step towards strengthening international cooperation for the preservation, study and wider dissemination of India's manuscript heritage, while creating new opportunities for scholarly and technological collaboration.

sum.text:
A Turkish parliamentary committee on Tuesday approved a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan amid growing tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The agreement requires the three countries to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three. Opposition parties, however, warned that the pact could draw Trkiye into conflicts involving other countries.
The foreign affairs committee approved the agreement with the support of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party and its allies despite opposition objections. It will now be debated and put to a vote in the full assembly, though no date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defence Agreement also allows military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. According to the agreement published by Turkish state media, the pact will remain in force for 10 years.
Ministers from the three countries have already met twice, in Istanbul and Riyadh. High-level delegations from the three nations also held talks in Tehran on Monday in an effort to prevent renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials said they were considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, PTI reported. However, they maintained that the agreement was defensive and that Turkish troops would not be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.
Fuat Oktay, a legislator from the ruling Justice and Development Party who heads the committee, urged members to approve the pact. He said it was aimed at strengthening deterrence and cooperation, did not target other countries and was likely to support peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries," Oktay said. "On the contrary, our nation is a party to defence agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability."
Opposition parties warned that the agreement could put Turkish soldiers at risk and involve the country in other nations' conflicts.
"Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Trkiye in the wars of other nations?" asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party.

sum.text:
New Delhi: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has issued an Advisory on ‘Women’s Safety at Work and Public Spaces’ to the Secretaries of ten Union Ministries, the Chairperson, Railway Board and the Chief Secretaries/ Administrators of all States and Union Territories. The NHRC notes that despite the existence of stringent laws to protect the rights of women, their safety at workplaces and public spaces remains a concern. As per the recent Periodic Labour Force Participation Survey in India, women’s participation in the labour force stood at 34.6% in September 2026.
However, about 4.4 lakh cases of crimes against women were also reported, as per the latest National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) report published in 2026. These figures underscore the persistent challenges in ensuring the safety and security of women and highlight the need for sustained and concerted efforts. It further notes that safety at workplaces and public spaces is an essential condition to enable women to participate fully in the workforce and realise their full potential. Besides the Railway Board, the Union Ministries to whom the Advisory has been sent include Women and Child Development, Education, Home Affairs, Information and Broadcasting, Labour and Employment, Corporate Affairs, Road Transport and Highways, Housing and Urban Affairs and Health and Family Welfare. The NHRC Advisory focuses on eight key areas.
These include raising awareness on topics of women’s safety and sexual harassment, infrastructure, encouraging bystander intervention, the role of the police, survivor support, cybercrime against women, long-term reforms and other measures. The declaration was announced by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and pledged to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations.
It also condemned the imposition of unilateral economic and secondary sanctions due to their negative implications on human rights.
The Forum supported comprehensive reform of the United Nations and its Security Council to make them more representative and efficient.
It condemned the terrorist attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, on 22 April 2025, which killed 26 people.
The declaration called for the expeditious adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework.
It reaffirmed adherence to sovereign equality, mutual respect, and non-intervention in internal affairs enshrined in the UN Charter.
The Forum supported the peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and expressed deep concern over West Asia tensions.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (PTI) The two-day conclave of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum on Tuesday adopted a joint declaration strongly condemning the 2025 Pahalgam attack and all acts of terrorism as it pledged to combat the menace in all its forms and manifestations and also stressed on non-intervention in the internal affairs of any country.
The joint declaration, announced by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, also condemned the imposition of unilateral economic and secondary sanctions saying such coercive measures have far reaching negative implications on human rights, including the right to development, health and food security of people.
The BRICS Parliamentary Forum supported a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council, saying this reform should make it more just, equitable, democratic, representative, effective, and efficient, better reflecting contemporary realities and the needs of the international community.
"We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir (in Pahalgam) on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.
"We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens," the declaration read.
The Forum said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.
"We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. We emphasise the primary responsibility of States in combating terrorism and that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must fully comply with their obligations under international law, including the Charter of the UN...," it read.
The Forum said it looks forward to further deepening counter-terrorism cooperation and calls for an expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework and concerted actions against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (IANS) India firmly believes that sporting excellence must always be accompanied by integrity, Minister of Youth Affairs & Sports Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya told the COP10 Bureau and a panel of the UNESCO International Convention against Doping in Sport.
Dr. Mandaviya chaired the third formal meeting of the COP10 Bureau and the fourth formal meeting of the Fund’s Approval Committee for 2026–27 under the UNESCO International Convention against Doping in Sport in New Delhi on Tuesday and assured the participants of India’s commitment to clean sport.
“Every athlete deserves a fair opportunity to compete, with success determined by talent, preparation and hard work, and not by prohibited substances or methods. Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi ji has regularly emphasised clean sport and the need to practice zero tolerance towards the menace of doping,” said Dr. Mandaviya.
The Union Sports Minister highlighted the strengthening of India’s anti-doping framework through the National Anti-Doping Act, 2022, and its 2025 Amendment.
“India has strengthened its legal and institutional framework through the National Anti-Doping Act, 2022, and its 2025 Amendment, both of which came into force in July 2026,” said Dr. Mandaviya. “We will also bring another amendment in the next session of our parliament, which aims to introduce criminal provisions to deal with violations even more effectively, including those by coaches and supply chain stakeholders.”
The Union Sports Minister further highlighted the steps India has already taken to tackle doping and inform its athletes about banned substances.
“During 2025-26, the National Anti-Doping Agency of India conducted over 7,000 tests and more than 350 education and awareness sessions, reaching 27,000 participants, while focusing on risk-based testing and intelligence-led investigations,” said Dr. Mandaviya. "The Know Your Medicine mobile application has recorded over half a million searches, supporting informed decisions about medicines.”
Dr. Mandaviya highlighted the forthcoming signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Ministry of Education, and UNESCO to introduce the Sport Values in Every Classroom Toolkit in India. The initiative aims to bring sporting values, ethics and integrity to classrooms and reach millions of young minds.

sum.text:
On 27 October 2026, Sarvam signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS) under the Ministry of Defence. The agreement sets an umbrella framework for artificial intelligence (AI) projects across the Indian Army, Indian Navy, Indian Air Force , and joint, tri-service and integrated organisations under HQ IDS.
Under the agreement, Sarvam will design, develop and deploy AI applications, and provide technical support for them. The applications will address operational, training and decision-support requirements of the three Services. HQ IDS will facilitate projects undertaken across the Services and participating joint organisations.
The agreement gives the Services access to shared foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems. A foundation model is an AI model trained on broad data that can be adapted for different tasks. Agentic infrastructure supports AI systems that can carry out tasks through a sequence of actions. Geospatial systems process information linked to locations, while perception systems interpret inputs such as images or other sensor data.
The stated areas of work include decision support, target acquisition and data fusion across the sensor-to-shooter loop. Target acquisition involves locating and identifying a potential target. Data fusion combines information from multiple sources, including sensors. The sensor-to-shooter loop covers the chain from detecting a target to engaging it. Human oversight will be retained over operational decisions.
The collaboration is intended to develop an AI layer for the armed forces with Indian partners and deploy it on sovereign infrastructure. Sarvam’s national security and defence division, Chanakya , will carry out the work using the company’s AI stack, including its Sarvam 105B foundation model. The MoU is aligned with the government’s Atmanirbharta in defence initiative.
Important Facts for Exams The Indian Armed Forces comprise the Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Air Force . HQ IDS provides an integrated framework for joint, tri-service defence organisations. points: The Government of India has introduced a Concessional Local Pass for non-commercial vehicle owners residing within 20 km of a national highway fee plaza.
The new provision aims to ease daily commuting costs and enhance the Ease of Living for residents living near toll plazas.
The scheme comes into effect from November 1, 2026, offering an annual pass option instead of the existing monthly pass.
The annual fee is fixed at Rs 1,500 for plazas outside municipal areas and Rs 3,000 for those within municipal limits.
Eligible vehicle owners must have a valid and functional FASTag to opt for the pass, which is restricted to a specific plaza.
The concessional pass is not available on highways using a closed user-fee collection system or where alternative service roads exist.
The passes will be available directly at eligible toll plazas from November 1, 2026, and via the Rajmargyatra App from December 1, 2026.
The central government may revise the rates annually, with changes taking effect from April 1 under the National Highways Act, 1956.

sum.text:
New Delhi: India has invited Pakistan’s Minister for National Heritage and Culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, to attend the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, the Hindu reports. The forum is scheduled to be held in the national capital from November 20 to 22, the publication reports, citing sources. However, Pakistan has not yet confirmed who will lead its delegation.
If Khichi attends, it will mark the first visit by a Pakistani minister to India since the SCO Foreign Ministers' meeting in Goa in May 2023. That year, Pakistan Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari had visited India. The forum would also be the first such ministerial visit since the four-day military conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025.
The Civilisational Dialogue Forum, as per the Hindu report, will be held at Purana Qila in Delhi and inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. It is being organised jointly by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs. The forum was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi inCulture ministers from all 10 member states, including Pakistan, China, Russia, Iran, Belarus and Central Asian countries have been invited, along with representatives from 15 dialogue partners and observer countries, the Hindu reports.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar visited Islamabad in November 2024 to represent India at the SCO Heads of Government meeting. India has not yet announced its level of representation at the SCO Heads of State Summit in Pakistan next year. India has continued participating in SCO activities despite suspending its participation in SAARC meetings in Islamabad since 2016.
In September 2026, India sent SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri to Islamabad for a coordination meeting related to Pakistan’s SCO presidency and preparations for the leaders’ summit scheduled to take place in Pakistan in August 2027.

The Nino3.4 index measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central tropical Pacific, serving as a primary indicator for El Nino.
The Indian Ocean Dipole is defined by the difference in sea surface temperatures between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean.
A positive Indian Ocean Dipole features warmer sea surface temperatures in the western Indian Ocean, often countering El Nino impacts in India.

Col Bertram Ang, Fleet Commander of the Republic of Singapore Navy, met RAdm Vishal Bishnoi to discuss mutual maritime interests.

sum.text:
October 27 (ANI): The 33rd edition of the Singapore-India Maritime Bilateral Exercise (SIMBEX-2026), hosted by the Indian Navy at Visakhapatnam, concluded on October 26. According to the Ministry of Defence, the exercise further strengthened the longstanding maritime cooperation and operational engagement between the Indian Navy and the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN). As part of the bilateral engagement, Colonel Bertram Ang, Fleet Commander of the RSN, called on RAdm Vishal Bishnoi, Flag Officer Commanding Eastern Fleet, and exchanged professional views on strengthening maritime cooperation between the two countries. The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss matters of mutual interest.
SIMBEX-2026 was conducted in two phases. The Harbour Phase featured Subject Matter Expert Exchanges (SMEEs), cross-deck visits, professional interactions, sporting engagements and planning conferences, facilitating the exchange of operational knowledge and enhancing mutual understanding. The Sea Phase in the Bay of Bengal involved Maritime Interdiction Operations, Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW), Anti-Air Warfare and Anti-Surface Warfare drills, seamanship evolutions and cross-deck flying operations, enhancing coordination and interoperability between the participating forces.
The exercise witnessed the participation of RSN ship RSS Supreme, a Formidable-class stealth frigate with an embarked SH-70B helicopter, the ministry said. The Indian Navy was represented by the indigenously built stealth frigate INS Nilgiri, ASW corvette INS Kamorta and participating aviation assets, including P-8I and Dornier maritime patrol aircraft, Hawk Advanced Jet Trainers and MH-60R helicopters. SIMBEX has served as an important platform for strengthening bilateral maritime cooperation, operational interoperability and professional engagement between India and Singapore. The exercise also demonstrated the commitment of both nations to enhancing maritime security and promoting stability in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). (ANI)

sum.text:
India, Oct. 27 -- The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), in collaboration with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA), will organise the launch of the book Timeless India: Protection & Revival of Indian Cultural Identity under the Leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, at 3:00 PM at Dharohar Bhawan, Archaeological Survey of India, Mandi House, New Delhi.
Published by IGNCA and Subhi Publication, the book will focus on India's rich cultural heritage, its historic monuments and the importance of preserving the country's civilisational legacy. It will explore themes concerning the protection and revival of Indian cultural identity, highlighting the significance of safeguarding the nation's heritage and historical memory. Shri Tarun Vijay, distinguished author, journalist and former Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha), is the author/editor of the book.
The occasion will be graced by Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Union Minister of Culture and Tourism, Government of India, as the Chief Guest. Dr. Jitendra Singh, Union Minister of State for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences, Government of India, will be the Guest of Honour. Dr. Vinay Sahasrabuddhe, former Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) and former President of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), will deliver the keynote address.
The programme will commence with a welcome address by Shri Y. S. Rawat, Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, followed by an opening address by Prof. (Dr.) Ramesh C. Gaur, Dean, Faculty of Arts, Media and Design, South Asian University. Shri Tarun Vijay will also be present at the launch in his capacity as the author/editor of the book. The programme will conclude with a vote of thanks by Prof. K. Anil Kumar, Head of Department, Kala Nidhi Division, IGNCA.
The launch will bring together distinguished guests, scholars and representatives from the cultural and heritage sectors to reflect on the importance of preserving India's historical monuments, cultural traditions and civilisational heritage. The occasion will also provide an opportunity to engage with the themes explored in the publication and their relevance to the preservation of India's cultural identity.

The Uttar Pradesh Cabinet on Tuesday approved plans to establish a robotics and artificial intelligence park in Greater Noida, build four link expressways spanning about 322 km and construct residential units for Allahabad High Court officers. The first, spread over eight acres, will be developed and operated through a special purpose vehicle under the public-private partnership model. The Greater Noida Authority will hold a 26% stake in the SPV, while the selected private industrial partner will own the remaining 74%. The Greater Noida Authority will contribute ₹21.1 crore as equity, while the state government will provide an interest-free loan of ₹126.2 crore for 30 years. The second zone, covering 61.52 acres, will be developed by private enterprises investing in industrial units and related activities. The state government will have no capital expenditure liability for this zone. The park will include shared facilities such as robotics testing and certification centres, rapid prototyping facilities, AI computing infrastructure, motion-capture systems and data laboratories. sum.text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday, October 27, reserved its judgment on a PIL seeking tighter regulation of medicine prices, questioning why a uniform trade margin cap of 16% cannot be imposed across drugs and sharply criticising private hospitals for charging steep mark-ups on medicines sold to patients. During the hearing, the court took exception to private hospitals' argument that higher margins on medicines help offset losses arising from government health schemes and insurance reimbursements. SC calls hospital mark-ups 'dacoity'The bench described such a practice as "dacoity" and said hospitals cannot subsidise their operations by overcharging patients.
It added that grievances over delayed or inadequate payments under government schemes should be raised with the authorities concerned. The Centre opposed blanket price controls, telling the court that a uniform cap on drug prices is not the answer and could hurt growth in the pharmaceutical industry. The government argued that India already has among the lowest medicine prices in the world and said policy decisions must balance affordability with investment and innovation.
According to the government, its approach towards the sector rests on four pillars: availability of medicines, innovation, industry growth and employment. It also maintained that competitive market forces should be allowed to function within a level playing field. Hospitals defend in-house pharmacy modelPrivate hospitals defended their in-house pharmacy model, saying they cannot permit medicines sourced from outside because they cannot guarantee their safety and quality.
During the proceedings, hospitals also acknowledged that a drug sold for about ₹30 in the open market could be priced at around ₹100 within hospital premises. Hospitals further argued that many beds are occupied by patients covered under government schemes, insurance programmes and the Central Government Health Scheme , where reimbursements are often lower than costs. They said adequate margins are necessary to invest in modern equipment and new medical services.
Responding to CNBC-TV18, pharma major Cipla said the debate around making medicines more affordable is an ongoing one and that the ultimate objective should be to make healthcare affordable for patients. The company, however, declined to comment on the recommendations relating to a uniform 16% trade margin cap and any proposed cap on maximum retail prices , citing the ongoing policy discussion. points: The Maharashtra cabinet approved a Rs 7,500 crore provision to provide advance financial assistance of Rs 5,000 each to eligible farmers ahead of Diwali.
The decision aims to provide immediate financial support to farmers in drought-hit regions while crop damage assessments continue.
The core issue involves mitigating agrarian distress and crop failure caused by drought conditions across multiple talukas in the state.
Around 1.5 crore farmers in 304 drought-hit talukas whose crops suffered more than 33 percent damage are eligible for the advance payment.
The financial assistance will be transferred directly to the bank accounts of beneficiaries through the Direct Benefit Transfer system.

sum.text:
MUMBAI: The Maharashtra cabinet on Tuesday approved a Rs 7,500 crore provision to provide advance financial assistance of Rs 5,000 each to eligible farmers in 304 drought-hit talukas across the state ahead of Diwali.
The Rs 5000 financial assistance is expected to benefit around 1.5 crore farmers, and this amount will be transferred directly to their bank accounts through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system.
Under the scheme, farmers in the 304 drought-hit taluks whose crops have suffered more than 33 per cent damage will be eligible for the advance payment.
The state administration has also initiated survey to finalise the crop damage assessments and area-wise details to determine the assistance payable to affected farmers. The advance payment is intended to provide immediate financial support ahead of the Diwali festival while the assessment and relief process continues.
To simplify the disbursement process, farmers who completed their electronic Know Your Customer (e-KYC) verification under various government schemes between November 1, 2025, and the date of the announcement will not be required to repeat the process.
The government has also made a special provision for farmers cultivating land under forest leases who have not yet received their Agristack Farmer Identification Number (Farmer ID). These farmers will be eligible for advance assistance based on their e-KYC.
Additionally, the state government has announced the fourth farm loan waiver list, which will benefit 4,15,000 farmers. Maharashtra State Cooperation Department has submitted a proposal to the finance department seeking Rs 4,000 crore for the loan waiver of these beneficiaries.
The scheme provides for a waiver of eligible outstanding crop loans of up to Rs 2 lakh, subject to prescribed conditions. Marathwada accounts for the largest reported share of beneficiaries, with around 6.27 lakh farmers receiving loan waiver benefits.
The Maharashtra cabinet also discussed complaints about finance companies allegedly harassing farmers over loan repayments. Shiv Sena Ministers reportedly called for strict action against companies found to be intimidating farmers facing financial distress.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (IANS) India is negotiating free trade agreements (FTAs) with several countries and groups with talks with Chile 'quite ripe' for conclusion and negotiations with Canada making good progress, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said.
During his two-day Netherlands visit, he told reporters that negotiations with the South Africa-led Southern African Customs Union (SACU) have started.
The two sides inked terms of reference (ToR) in August to formally start negotiations towards a preferential trade agreement.
However, the five members of SACU are Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa.
"I can see Chile's quite ripe for conclusion; Canada is making very good progress. We have just started SACU negotiations, so it may take some time," Goyal said.
Talking about other pacts, he said Mexico is very keen to have an early harvest trade agreement.
Also, he expressed hope that continuity of government in Brazil following elections would help speed up negotiations to expand the Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) with the Mercosur bloc.
Apart from that, Goyal held meetings with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, Heleen Herbert, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate and Arthur van Dijk, King's Commissioner of North Holland.
He also interacted with members of the Dutch House of Representatives Committee on Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation and the Senate Committee on European Affairs to exchange perspectives on bilateral economic relations and the broader India-EU economic partnership.
An important segment was the India-Netherlands Business Forum jointly chaired by Goyal and Sjoerdsma which saw participation of about 200 people including leading Indian and Dutch businesses.
The forum focused on opportunities emerging from the India-EU FTA in expanding bilateral trade, strengthening investment partnerships and fostering collaboration.
Goyal also held one-to-one meetings with CEOs from Dutch companies across semiconductors, electronics, logistics, energy and retail, and participated in a roundtable with CXOs of 15 Dutch firms organised by the Indian Embassy in The Hague in collaboration with HSBC Netherlands.
He highlighted growing momentum in India-Netherlands ties following elevation to Strategic Partnership and conclusion of India-EU FTA, underscoring Netherlands' role as gateway to European markets.

A team of UNESCO and ICOMOS experts has inspected the historical monuments at Hampi and other heritage sites in Vijayanagara district, reviewing conservation measures, construction activities, tourism management and the livelihoods of local residents. The team is expected to submit its report within six weeks. The experts visited several historical monuments, including the Vijaya Vittala Temple, Krishna Temple, Lotus Mahal and Gagan Mahal, to assess their present condition and conservation requirements.
Vijayanagara Deputy Commissioner Kavitha S Mannikeri told reporters on Tuesday that the team, comprising UNESCO expert George Abungu and ICOMOS expert Ishita Shimoda, held discussions with officials of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and reviewed the condition of major monuments and the measures taken for their conservation. She said the team also examined construction activities around Anjanadri Hill, the expansion of commercial establishments and arrangements for managing the increasing number of tourists visiting the region. The experts stressed the need to ensure that construction and other development activities do not obstruct the views of historical monuments or affect the heritage character of Hampi.
They also suggested measures to preserve Hampi as a living cultural heritage site. An important aspect of the discussions was the need to protect the livelihoods of people living in and around the heritage area while implementing conservation measures. The experts suggested preparing a comprehensive master plan that would balance the protection of historical monuments with the interests of local communities.
The discussions covered the concerns of tourist guides, autorickshaw drivers, hotel workers, priests, farmers and local artists whose livelihoods depend directly or indirectly on activities in the heritage area. Issues relating to restrictions on construction and other activities in the core heritage zone, protection of houses and properties belonging to local residents, movement of tourists and the operation of homestays were also discussed, the DC stated. The projects span 410 km across eight districts in West Bengal, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh and are aimed at enhancing rail capacity, easing congestion and improving operational efficiency and service reliability.
The approved projects include the Kharagpur-Bhadrak (Ranital) fourth line covering 173 km across West Bengal and Odisha, the Bhadrak-Haridaspur fourth line of 75 km in Odisha, the Gummidipundi-Gudur third and fourth lines spanning 90 km across Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and the Cuttack-Paradeep (Badabandha) third and fourth lines of 72 km in Odisha.
These projects are being implemented under the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan with a focus on integrated planning and stakeholder consultations to strengthen multimodal connectivity and improve logistics efficiency.
The capacity augmentation is expected to ensure smoother movement of passengers, goods and services while reducing congestion and improving the overall efficiency of train operations. The addition of these lines will expand the railway network by about 410 km and improve connectivity to around 6,448 villages with a combined population of nearly 60 lakh.
The enhanced rail infrastructure is also expected to strengthen connectivity to several tourist and religious destinations, including Kuldiha Wildlife Sanctuary, Bhitarkanika National Park, Maa Bhadrakali Temple, Maa Dhamarai Temple, Panchalingeswar Temple, Talsari-Udaypur and Chandipur beaches, Pulicat Lake, Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary, Lord Veeraraghava Perumal Temple, Gada Kujanga Jagannath Temple, Sarala Temple, Dhabaleswar Temple and Lalitgiri, a prominent Buddhist site.
The routes play a key role in transporting essential commodities such as coal, iron ore, cement, iron and steel, containers, automobiles and foodgrains, supporting industrial and economic activity across the regions.
The government has stated that the projects are expected to generate additional freight traffic of around 76 million tonnes per annum (MTPA).
